speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seek the unanimous consent of the House under Standing Order 43 to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, that is the very uncertain position of beef producers.
Since beef producers in Eastern Canada are slaughtering cattle day after day on or along the roads for the purpose of drawing the government's attention to their difficulties arising from an increase in production costs and a decline in beef prices, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House examine immediately the disastrous situation in which beef producers are now, and that recommendations be made in order to take immediate steps to protect those producers and thus spare the consumer difficulties arising in a few months.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-360, an act to amend the Criminal Code.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT JUVENILES FROM INVITATIONS TO ENGAGE IN SEXUAL ACTS
speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROTECT JUVENILES FROM INVITATIONS TO ENGAGE IN SEXUAL ACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill will amend the Criminal Code to fill the gap created by a recent decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal. Before that decision an offender could be convicted, if found guilty, of making an indecent proposition to a child under 15 years of age if the offence were proven. The decision had the effect of requiring some physical touching to complete the offence. The amendment will restore the former law and give extra protection to children.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REASON FOR MEETING WITH PREMIERS-PROPOSALS BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REASON FOR MEETING WITH PREMIERS-PROPOSALS BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the right hon. Prime Minister in connection with his meeting tomorrow with the premiers of the provinces. I am very pleased that this meeting is to take place. In view of the fact that the Prime Minister rejected the request for such a meeting a few weeks ago and now has invited the premiers to come to Ottawa tomorrow, can he tell the House what the new

development is that makes the meeting seem worthwhile now when it seemed to him to be worthless just a few weeks ago?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REASON FOR MEETING WITH PREMIERS-PROPOSALS BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure what the Leader of the Opposition is referring to in terms of what happened a few weeks ago. If he is referring to the idea proposed by Premier Davis in a speech he made at the Toronto Ex when he talked of a public summit, that is the idea I rejected. I have never rejected the idea of consultation; on the contrary, it was very much part of our policy. We talked about it in the Speech from the Throne and I have talked about it at various places publicly and about the importance of talking with all sectors of the Canadian public, including provincial governments.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REASON FOR MEETING WITH PREMIERS-PROPOSALS BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Whatever request may have been made by a particular premier, it was an informal meeting that all the premiers requested following their own meeting. I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether it is intended tomorrow to put before the premiers a specific proposal with regard to the forum and the method of consultation which the government of Canada intends to pursue in order to see whether any consensus can be achieved among the principal groups in our economy as to how the GNP should be divided.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REASON FOR MEETING WITH PREMIERS-PROPOSALS BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the best way I can answer this is to indicate the process of consultation which we have always had in mind was an ongoing one; one which would proceed step by step. I would not want to convey to the House the idea that tomorrow we will make any kind of proposition to the provincial premiers. We have announced in the Speech from the Throne that there will be a federal-provincial conference with the premiers early in the new year. The precise type of proposal that the Leader of the Opposition is talking about would be better made then than tomorrow. Tomorrow is the beginning of a process in so far as the premiers's consultations with me are concerned.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REASON FOR MEETING WITH PREMIERS-PROPOSALS BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: A final supplementary, Mr. Speaker. I must say the Prime Minister's casual approach to the question of inflation is shocking to me.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REASON FOR MEETING WITH PREMIERS-PROPOSALS BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REASON FOR MEETING WITH PREMIERS-PROPOSALS BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Order, order!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REASON FOR MEETING WITH PREMIERS-PROPOSALS BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE BORROWING POWER OF COMPANIES AND AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF SUBORDINATED NOTES

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE BORROWING POWER OF COMPANIES AND AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF SUBORDINATED NOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes to make certain amendments to the Trust Companies Act and the Loan Companies Act. These statutes provide for the incorporation and supervision of federally-incorporated trust companies and mortgage loan companies, respectively.

October 29, 1974
Trust Companies Act
Trust companies raise money from the public by accepting deposits and selling guaranteed investment certificates. Loan companies obtain their funds by the sale of debentures and the acceptance of deposits. For both types of companies the relevant statute places a maximum limit on the funds that can be obtained from the public. At present, this maximum limit is 20 times the company's capital and surplus, which can only be reached with the approval of the minister. The effect of these limits is to require the maintenance of at least a minimum excess of assets over liabilities to the public. This provides a safety margin in the sense that any asset losses can be absorbed first by this excess before any question arises as to the ability of the company to meet its obligations.
The maximum limit on the amount that any trust or loan company may borrow from the public was raised in 1970 from 15 to 20 times a company's capital and surplus. However, because of the rapid expansion being experienced by these companies, a number of them are now reaching the new limit. As a result, the companies requested that the existing capital margins be modified to enable them to continue to expand.
The government recognizes that a number of trust and loan companies are sufficiently sound, financially and from the standpoint of management, to justify some expansion beyond existing limits as previously referred to. In this bill we are, therefore, proposing that the Trust Companies Act and the Loan Companies Act be amended to permit a trust or loan company to borrow-in the case of trust companies it is more accurate to say that they accept money from the public in trust-in excess of 20 times a company's capital and surplus, subject to the adoption of an enabling bylaw establishing a new limit, which bylaw would have to be approved by the minister.
The authority to exceed the limit will also be subject to the ability of the company to meet a number of financial criteria that will be established by regulations. The amendment proposed would also empower the minister to require, as a condition of approving the borrowing bylaw, that some proportion of the additional borrowings in excess of the present limits be in the form of subordinated notes. This is desirable to ensure that a company retains an adequate margin of protection for, first, depositors; second, the holders of guaranteed investment certificates; and third, the holders of ordinary debentures.
As I have mentioned, the issuance of subordinated notes is part and parcel of the increased borrowing limits, and the bill would therefore expand the corporate powers of the companies to enable them to issue such subordinated notes subject to certain limitations designed to avoid confusion between the subordinated notes and any other instrument the company might issue to the public. I should mention here that these notes are intended primarily for sale to institutional investors and will only be issued in denominations of $25,000 or more.
Because of the rapidity. with which events seem to change in the financial world in current years, it is desirable to have some slight flexibility in the application of these limits. Because of rapidly increasing deposits or a drop in security values, a company may find itself at or

near its limits more quickly than might be expected. In order to provide some time to the company to arrange for additional capital or a modification of its pattern of growth, the bill contains two provisions that would, in certain circumstances, permit a company to accept funds in excess of limits otherwise applicable.
The first of these provisions relates to the amount off highly liquid assets, cash and government bonds, held by a company. A company would be given authority to accept funds from the public in excess of limits otherwise prescribed, to the extent that its highly liquid assets exceed the minimum prescribed by the act. The other special provision is that under terms and conditions prescribed by the minister, funds received by way of a loan from a shareholder or shareholders may be treated as though they were part of the capital for purposes of computing the limit on funds accepted from the public, provided the loan is made on terms subordinated to all other indebtedness of the company. It would be expected that the terms and conditions prescribed by the minister would be such as to make the use of subordinated loans in this way a temporary expedient to be replaced by permanent capital at an early date.
It occasionally happens that a company may find itself in excess of the limits imposed by the provisions of the act. Should this happen, the Superintendent of Insurance is required to report to the minister, and the minister may prescribe a time within which the company is to remedy the defect, he may impose conditions on the company or, in an extreme case, he may direct the superintendent to take control of the company's assets.
Some question has been raised concerning the obligation of a company toward its depositors and creditors in respect of funds received during a period that it is in excess of the limits otherwise prescribed. To remove any doubt on this score, the bill makes clear that in such case a company's obligations are not affected by the fact that it is in excess of those limits.
It is in the public interest that the amendments proposed by this bill be adopted, since trust companies and mortgage loan companies are an important source of funds for residential mortgages. The additional funds that these amendments, if passed, would allow them to raise would, of course, enable the companies to expand their lending activities while maintaining their financial stability. It might be of interest to note that at the end of 1973 there were 17 federally-incorporated trust companies with total assets exceeding $3.5 billion. This includes company funds and funds received in trust, the repayment of which is guaranteed. There were, as well, 14 mortgage loan companies with aggregate assets of approximately $3.25 billion.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE BORROWING POWER OF COMPANIES AND AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF SUBORDINATED NOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a preliminary matter before speaking to the actual bill. My suggestion might help to facilitate the business of this House. This bill was given third reading in the other place last Thursday or Friday. It was studied in a committee of the other place. Unfortunately, it will not be possible for us to obtain a transcript of the evidence taken before that committee until the end of this week. I know the purpose of the government, and commend it for initiating this kind of legislation in the other place. I think the Senate Committee on Banking and Commerce can do
October 29, 1974

an admirable job of investigating, questioning, and so on, with respect to legislation. The transcript of evidence taken before that committee would help hon. members of this House, in the same way as evidence taken before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs is helpful to hon. senators. But to be helpful we must have those transcripts. Efforts must be made to speed up their release.
Owing to the change in the scheduling of this bill, backbenchers both on this side and that of the government are at some disadvantage in that we do not have the benefit of knowing what happened in the other place. I hope the government will initiate more bills there and I commend the government House leader for what he has done. However, I ask him to keep in mind what I have said and have someone on his staff see that transcripts of evidence from Senate committees come forward as soon as possible so we can use them.
My second point also concerns scheduling. This bill is to be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. Government supporters on that committee should be interested in the bill and may want to hear this debate, but they are dealing with another bill this afternoon. The government has asked them to do this. The committee was supposed to sit tonight but for some reason the sitting was advanced to this afternoon. Three or four members of my party who should be attending that committee, which is dealing with the Federal Business Development Bank Act, cannot attend; they must remain in the House to deal with this particular bill. I ask for closer scheduling of these matters.
I also wish to comment on the order of business and I draw my remarks to the attention of the government House leader. I am referring to the many bills referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; there is a long queue of them. I do not think we are advancing House business simply by passing bills in this chamber and referring them to that committee, where they must remain queued up. Other House committees have nothing to do at present, and legislation could and should be referred to them. I know that this is sometimes difficult to arrange. In the previous session of parliament, of the first nine items six were sent to the finance committee. It had difficulty doing its work and government supporters on the committee and members from the opposition were very hard pressed.
Let me turn my attention to Bill S-7. Frankly, I wonder why the government has brought forward this bill at this time. It is some time since there was an examination of the business of banking and of the granting of credit in Canada. In view of rapidly changing events, and as conditions in the 1970s are far removed from those of the 1950s, I would expect the government to set up another commission of inquiry of the nature of the Porter royal commission on banking, which was set up almost 15 years ago. True, its findings were not handed down until 1964, but these things take time. I suggest that the government should give earnest consideration to again setting up such an inquiry, if the new Bank Act which I have discussed is to be brought in by 1977.
I do not think the public, the banking system or the government have sufficient information on hand to bring
Trust Companies Act
down the type of Bank Act we shall need in 1977. Conditions have changed immensely since the time amendments to the Bank Act were brought forward following the report of the Porter commission. I remember when the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp), then minister of finance, brought forward those amendments. Even then I was concerned about a good deal of the philosophy embodied in the changes, even though the Bank Act was out of date. However, there were some steps forward.
With the greatest respect, all the government is doing with this bill is tinkering with one or two bolts in the machinery of credit granting and banking. After all, these trust companies do engage in the business of banking. We are not dealing with their powers as executors or their powers as mortgage companies to invest in realty mortgages. At this point we are dealing with the concept of a trust company as a credit granting institution. There is no way anyone can put it any other way; a trust company does engage in the business of banking.
As I said, this bill is a mere tinkering with a couple of bolts of the machine. It is not as serious as the tinkering that is proposed in Bill C-7, where there is quite a fundamental change of philosophy by introduction of the notion of partial public ownership in our chartered banks. That is something quite new, quite different; but it is tinkering of the worst kind. It represents moves now and then which are unrelated. Our entire credit granting and banking system in this country is far too complicated and far too important to engage in any of this ad hoc, unscheduled, uncoordinated tinkering.
Bill C-7 is only window-dressing in response to the premier of one province-possibly the premiers of two- having a delusion or illusion of grandeur. They feel they should be able to move in on one or more of the chartered banks. If and when Bill C-7 comes forward, we will have plenty to say about it. However, I feel this is a wrong step by the government in principle and philosophy in its strategy to deal with the banking system of Canada.
The parliamentary secretary was quite correct-there is no pretension of the legislation holding out more. This legislation will affect only trust companies falling under federal jurisdiction. In number they are small compared with the totality of trust companies operating in Canada. The biggest trust companies are not under federal jurisdiction. For example, the Royal Trust Company and the Montreal Trust Company escape the direct jurisdiction of federal legislation because they are provincially-incor-porated trust companies. True enough, there is some indirect control over them through the deposit insurance regulations, but that is a very untidy and improper way of dealing with the situation. These companies engage in the business of banking. My answer to this question is that there should be a general banking act defining the business of banking. Anyone, whether incorporated provincially or federally, would then have to submit to the jurisdiction of the act.
The Superintendent of Banking should be a much more active official, not merely a passive receiver of information from our financial institutions. We should have a much wider banking system which would permit mer-

October 29, 1974
Trust Companies Act
chant banking, for example. This would do away with the "suitcase banking" that has been going on in many areas. Foreign banks operate through agents coming into Canada as visitors; they set up in a hotel room. They are engaged in the business of banking in Canada but are totally beyond the reach of the Minister of Finance or any supervisory agency of the government. Something is wrong when we have this situation.
It seems to me there is a proper way to deal with these matters, and I will come back to this point time and time again. I thought I had the minister of finance of the day at least partly persuaded in 1965 and 1966 that we should have a general banking act with appropriate sections or portions applicable to our chartered banks. They are a category of banks. I would also like to see merchant banks and trust companies, in their banking functions, controlled under such an act. At the present time we do not have the necessary flexible instruments in Canada. The lack of flexibility is clearly pointed out by this attempt to introduce a degree of flexibility of formula with regard to expansion of the lending powers of trust and loan companies.
However, there is one point here that I do not like. There is no specific control on the limit of overborrowing by trust companies. It is at the discretion of the minister. Parliament is being asked to give a blank cheque. What will motivate the minister to exercise his discretion? How will there be any certainty in so far as the operations of trust or loan companies are concerned, which are, presumably, supposed to benefit from this feature of flexibility? Who is to determine who receives the favourable discretion of the minister? Is not overlimit borrowing providing a sort of bail-out mechanism by permitting an increase in debt? In the recent history of the United States permission was given to borrow over the limit in order to assist with a bail-out. However, it did not work.
There are, supposedly, regulations to determine the financial health of a company; however, these are not specified. There is no indication of the regulations. Without wishing to go into detail, I am dumbfounded by their range. We are being asked to pass this open-ended legislation without having a chance to see the regulations. It is possible we shall have the opportunity of learning at least something of the nature of the regulations in committee. In fact, the regulations may well have been drafted and it may be possible to submit them to the committee, as has been done in the past with legislation of this kind.
Here again, we are considering an increase in the lending and borrowing powers of loan and trust companies which are beyond the control of the Bank of Canada. This is strange. The government already finds it difficult to maintain adequate monetary control at this time of inflation, but the bill before us proposes extending the powers of institutions over whose operations it has little or no control as far as monetary policy is concerned. It gives them a free hand. The parliamentary secretary might care to comment on this point, or tell us that the Minister of Finance will have something to say about it. I think it is one which should be considered by the government even though the margin might in the over-all be negligible.

As I say, I do not want to go into detail now. A number of my hon. friends will have something more to say about this bill which was approved rather quickly in the other place. It will be some time before we reach it in our committee. I hope that later today we will complete this discussion and send the bill to committee. But that is the only undertaking I shall make at this time.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE BORROWING POWER OF COMPANIES AND AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF SUBORDINATED NOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us is to authorize federal loan and trust companies to increase the monetary limit of their borrowing power. As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said at the outset, it applies only to companies incorporated under federal law. As far as I know, that involves only 17 trust companies with assets of $3.5 billion, and 14 loan companies with assets of $3.25 billion. So we are considering corporations with assets of slightly under $7 billion, according to the latest information I have received.
I wonder why this bill comes before us today, Mr. Speaker. It originated in the other place. I shall ask some serious questions about this measure and attempt to discover the motivation behind bringing it before the House of Commons at this time. Some of the information I have would lead me to believe that these trust and loan companies have been lobbying the government to get the legislation passed because their profit picture has been suffering. They are finding it necessary to pay more for money, and they are locked into mortgage contracts with low interest rates and five-year terms which they cannot escape. As a result, they are caught in a squeeze and their profits are not rising. If borrowing limits are removed, they can obtain more money and lend it at higher interest rates to compensate for the fact that a great deal of capital is tied up at lower rates. The fact that profits have been falling is one of the strongest motivations behind the presentation of this legislation.
The second reason for the bill is that trust and loan companies want to strengthen their place in the mortgage market. They have dominated that market for a number of years. Today, the supply of money is tighter; they want access to more funds; they want the ceiling to be raised so they can continue to dominate the market. This is an approach to which members of my party do not take very kindly. We believe that the federal government, representing the people, should be pumping millions and millions of dollars into the mortgage market at a low interest rate of, say, 6 per cent for people in the low or middle income groups. The money which the loan and trust companies are raising is going into the housing market at rates of 12 or 13 per cent, while interest rates on second mortgages are higher still.
The only motivation for putting this bill before us today is to fatten the profits of the trust and loan companies and to enable their shareholders to reap benefits at the expense of the consumer and the home builder. This bill will help to keep inflation rates high. It will help to drive up interest rates and keep inflation going. If it is passed and the companies expand their operations, they will be obliged to pay higher interest rates to depositors and bond subscribers in order to obtain more capital to lend. Corresponding rates of interest must then be charged on loans if desired profit rates are to be maintained. In other rates,
October 29, 1974

inflation will be reinforced and prospective Canadian home buyers will find their situation increasingly difficult.
I cannot see any reason at all why I, as a person who tries to represent the consumer, should support this bill. The only people who will gain through its passage are shareholders in the trust and loan companies. The hon. member for Edmonton West has drawn attention to other reasons why the House should view with concern the passage of this measure. We are asked to give a blank cheque to trust and loan companies in order to create more money during a time of inflation. I know the regulations will set out guidelines, but how will those guidelines be interpreted? This will be left to the Minister of Finance. No ceiling will be placed on the amount of new money which will be created. I do not like this sort of situation being created in a highly inflationary situation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the bill originated in a very undemocratic, corporate lobby-namely, the Senate. I do not like the idea of bills coming to this House from the other place. The position taken by members of my party is clear. The other chamber is a place to which members are not elected but are appointed until age 75. This goes against the grain.
When this bill was considered by the other place last week, the president of the Trust Companies Association of Canada testified before the Senate committee and spoke of the need for the bill. He pretty well admitted that the prime motivation for the bill was to facilitate the making of greater profits by the trust and loan companies of this country, since so much money was being tied up in mortgages at a lower rate of interest that was prevalent a few years ago. Mr. D. G. Neelands, president of the Trust Companies Association of Canada and president of Canada Permanent Trust, had this to say:
The trust industry ... is experiencing sumc	the prcec-*
time in terms of earnings because of the effect that rapidly rising interest rates have on spread. This is a matter which is obviously outside the industry's control and really the only-or major-defensive action or counteraction that the industry can take is to increase its volume.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE BORROWING POWER OF COMPANIES AND AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF SUBORDINATED NOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Cullen) introduce this bill, and although I do not fault the hon. member for this, I found that the wording he put on the record was very strange. It was wording that could have been used 10 or 20 years ago, or perhaps in some other country today. For obvious reasons, the hon. member, or whoever wrote his remarks, chose to avoid talking about the real problems that are causing the government to introduce this bill.
The fact is that the government has tended, through its spending and monetary programs, to aggravate inflation in this country beyond reason. A consequence of this deliberate action is that trust and loan companies are finding it exceedingly difficult to remain competitive, to render the service that I suggest to the hon. member for the NDP who has just spoken they have been rendering, and at the same time to make a fair return, called a profit.

October 29, 1974
Trust Companies Act
I believe it is time we were a little more frank with the Canadian public.
Inflation today is a political problem, not an economic one. For the last four years the government has known perfectly well that steps should be taken to curb inflation in this country, yet it has chosen, I suggest egged on by NDP members, deliberately to throw out responsible fiscal and monetary measures of the kind that should have been implemented. As a result, the government has brought in a bill which, if you read between the lines, Mr. Speaker, is designed to correct the problems they know exist in a very substantial industry in Canada, namely, the trust and loan companies.
The figures are really startling. For example, the money supply in this country has doubled in four years. From the first quarter of 1970 to the first quarter of this year-the last available figures that I have-the money supply jumped from $12.5 billion to $25 billion. This is one of the root causes of inflation, and there is no way the government should be allowed to duck that fact. If one looks at the figures, one finds that trust and loan corporations have increased their assets, deposits and guaranteed certificates and debentures, along with most other financial institutions. However, I suggest-and I was very disappointed with the answer given me by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in this connection-that it is now time for the government to commission an outgoing study of the Canadian banking and financial system.
In 1961 such a study was aked for, and it led to the Porter commission on banking. I believe they made a worth-while review of the trust and loan field, the life insurance field, consumer banking and the other financial sectors of our economy. But let us put it in perspective. At that time the baking industry in Canada had gross assets of about $20 billion. Today they are over $80 billion-four times the amount. One bank today, the Royal Bank of Canada, is greater in size than the entire banking community at the time of the Porter commission on banking in the early 1960s. Trust companies, likewise, have had phenomenal growth, as have the loan companies in the same period. For example, in 1964 the trust companies had guaranteed funds of $2.6 billion; at the end of 1973 their guaranteed funds amounted to $9.8 billion.
The funds of estates, trusts and agencies handled by the trust companies rose in the same period from $11.2 billion to $29 billion. In total, the assets of trust companies in Canada rose from $14.1 billion in 1964 to $39.7 billion in
1973.	The mortgage companies, or loan companies as they were called, had a correspondingly sensational growth, although slightly slower than the growth to which I have referred.
I would point out that a heavy proportion of that growth has been due to the inflationary policies followed by this government. This is the reason we are debating a bill that proposes to raise the limit under which the trust and loan companies may operate with regard to their deposits, guaranteed investment certificates and, in the case of loan companies, debentures. Surely it is time, again, to ask whether our banking system is working properly. Is it proper to have ten chartered banks at the present time, 63

trust companies, and a smaller number of loan companies dealing in somewhat similar activities and yet not all under the same act and not controlled by the same regulatory authorities? This is a question which has been raised many times.
I believe it is important for this House to consider whether it is time our banking institutions and our trust and loan companies were treated in a way that would allow them to be in a truly competitive position. In that way we might find that the type of situation with which we are dealing today would not recur as readily. The truth is-this came out during the Senate committee hearings- that the banks do not have these artificial limits. For example, they do not have to meet a limit of 20 times their capital. Why do the trust and loan companies have to follow such arbitrary limits?
I believe we should be asking ourselves whether previous parliaments were totally wrong when they said that trust and loan companies should be limited to 4, 8, 12'A or 20 times their capital. Were they totally wrong, when today we say we should have a very much looser system which is not open to decision by this House but simply to future drafters of regulations and some discretionary overseeing by the minister? Who is wrong?
I suggest that over the last ten years this government has systematically ignored the rule-book in order to suit its own political purposes as far as economics are concerned. Once you have abandoned sound monetary and fiscal policies it is only natural that you must come in with band-aid legislation such as this to repair the damage done to institutions in our financial system which have been caught in a difficult position. This government likes to take comfort from the fact that other countries are also in a difficult inflationary position. Let us face it: why should the government not take comfort from this fact? If one looks at the predominant government parties in most of the industrialized countries since the end of the Second World War, one sees they have been socialist, liberal, or democratic governments of the left. It is 30 years since the legislatures of our main industrialized nations became dominated by liberal, socialist or democratic governments of the left, to which I have referred.
I think it should be placed on record that in the United States, for example, the Democratic Party has held a majority of seats in both the Senate and the House of Representatives for all but four of the past 40 years. In Great Britain, Labour has had a consistent edge over the Conservatives since 1945, while in Canada only once in the past 39 years has there been a majority Conservative government: that was in 1958. I could go on and give similar statistics in respect of other industrialized countries.
1 suggest there has been a consistent move toward irresponsible fiscal and monetary measures in those countries. That is why the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) can almost take heart when comparing his record to those of his socialist, liberal and democratic friends who are to the left, in other countries. They all follow a "no rules" system so far as management of their monetary and fiscal affairs is concerned. Let me be more specific. Surely we should be asking ourselves, when we consider this type of legislation, why the majority of the trust companies in this

country are under provincial, rather than federal, jurisdiction. If one looks at the individual trust companies in Canada, one finds that very few are under federal control. Our bigger trust companies are provincially controlled.
Here we have a situation in which a very important sector, as indicated by the billions of dollars in assets which the trust companies control, is not wholly controlled by the government of Canada. That is a further reason for believing a Porter-like commission on banking would be a suitable study, rather than the introduction of legislation such as we are considering today in virtual isolation from the other ingredients of our financial community. In this bill-I hope this matter will come out in committee-I think it is interesting to note that we still refer to things called assets and liabilities and that there are ratios under which, say, 20 times your excess of assets over liabilities is the limit.
What is meant by assets? In an inflationary economy such as the government has triggered, what value is placed on an NHA, 6 per cent mortgage that has 15 or 20 years to run? Is it fair to show that item on your balance-sheet on a cost, or even on an amortized basis, when you know the reality is that if the mortgage had to be sold immediately it would have nothing close to an amortized or cost value? A look at our trust and loan companies will show that they are still reflecting their mortgages on a cost basis-certainly at the Ottawa level.
When this bill is considered in committee, I hope the minister or the officials of his department will explain the current position with regard to trust and loan companies. Do they, in fact, have an excess of capital over liabilities if true value is taken into account? I refer to the liquidation value of their mortgage portfolios and any other assets they have which are subject to today's market fluctuations. I would also point out that if one reads the annual reports of the trust companies, one finds that over the last few years there has been increasingly a comment in the reports to the effect that tney nope me government will quickly take steps to end inflation which is causing them distinct problems.
Guaranty Trust's annual report, for example, pointed out very specifically that they felt it was regrettable that so many people were, in effect, apologizing for inflation instead of taking steps to end it. They and the other trust companies involved are well aware of the devastation that inflation is inflicting upon the country.
In conclusion, let me say that we know this bill will go to committee and we can do nothing about it, but I suggest that we in this House can do something about the irresponsible actions of the government with respect to the economy. I believe we should ask ourselves: was it really necessary for government expenditures in the past ten years to soar by 330 per cent, if you exclude defence expenditures? That 330 per cent increase does not include such matters as the sixfold increase in our unemployment insurance benefits. I mention this because the 330 per cent increase this government has brought about in its own spending has contributed to inflation. The increase they have allowed has caused inflation, yet if we review history

we find that the situation in which we are living is truly abnormal.
It is totally wrong for the government to indicate that somehow inflation is uncontrollable and that we must live with it. The fact is that you can go back literally 300 years in British history and you will find there never has been a period of inflation comparable to the present one, other than in wartime. Surely we must ask ourselves why, for a period of 110 years prior to the First World War, the industrialized countries of the world had a 3 per cent to 5 per cent interest rate structure, with very little inflation, and today we are told that we must accept a 10 per cent to 12 per cent interest rate structure, with a similar rate of inflation. The fact is that if this government had the courage, we could counteract inflation.
It seems to me that the type of bill with which we are dealing would not be necessary because the trust and loan companies could operate as well under a 20 times ceiling, without this type of escape valve, which would allow them to look after any immediate problems they may have as the result of inflationary pressures. I do not wish to delay the bill, but I hope we will at least undertake in committee a partial review of the situation. Most important, I urge the government, once again, to overview the entire financial system in Canada so that the whole country knows where it is going. I am very fearful of the direction in which the economy appears to be heading.

Speaker, the question will be put in due course, I am sure, and the bill will go to committee at the appropriate time. I am somewhat annoyed that we have not been given its background.
The Senate had meetings and hearings at which there were witnesses. As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out, we in this House are not given the opportunity to study the evidence presented to the Senate committee. Surely the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) could have put together some information for us so we could adequately examine the various facets of the bill.
This bill pertains only to trust and loan companies that are federally chartered, Madam Speaker, so the first thing we have to ask is, what about provincially-chartered companies? Has there been any liaison or discussion with the provinces on this matter? Are they going to bring forward parallel legislation in the near future? The activities of trust and loan companies figure very prominently in the monetary life of this country; they are a very powerful force.
Anyone in the mortgage field knows very well that these companies are in great difficulty today because of lack of funds. This legislation will allow them to increase their borrowings so that they will have the funds to lend. I cannot find fault with their having more funds, because one of the complaints from those who are concerned with housing in this country is that not enough mortgage funds are available. They claim this is creating the high interest rates we are faced with. So we can hope that if more funds become available, interest rates will come down and the housing market will be assisted.
My concern, Madam Speaker, is that we do not seem to know where we are going in the over-all banking field. Let us face the facts of life. Trust and loan companies are competing with the banks for deposits with which to operate their businesses. Across this country we have the chartered banks, 65 or 75 trust companies, a number of loan companies, credit unions, and venture capital firms of all kinds. It is obvious to anyone who has even a nodding acquaintance with the financial world that trust companies and banks are caught up in inflation. It is time, therefore, the minister considered setting up another royal commission on banking. Perhaps the way to start would be

with a preliminary inquiry conducted by the Senate, and then to have a full-blown royal commission.
Madam Speaker, I should like to quote from the 1973 annual report of the Guaranty Trust Company which indicates that company's concern. The report points out that we were faced, in 1972-73, with great legislative uncertainties. That is a polite way of saying they are very concerned about the level of inflation in this country and what is being done about it. The report opens by saying:
The 1972 report to the shareholders noted that, "with the large increase in money supply that has taken place in 1972 and the possibility of a continued substantial increase in 1973, there is a great danger of sharp increases in inflation and, therefore, interest rates-
The report refers to 1972 inflation rates, which were not nearly as high as they are today. I continue:
-as 1973 draws to a close and the third successive year of economic growth ends. It is possible that 1974 will see the end of the current cycle of growth and this may coincide with high inflation and high interest rates."
This assessment, while generally correct, did not anticipate the magnitude of the increase in both interest rates and inflation that faced the company this past year and that faces the company in the future.
As senior officers of a company which invests money on behalf of other people, we are concerned by the fact that so many people seem to be taking this rapid increase in inflation for granted. The Economic Council of Canada in its recent annual report said that Canada should merely outperform its neighbouring countries in this respect. So far, the country seems to be able to tolerate without any great social unrest a rate of inflation between 5 per cent and 8 per cent.
Inflation is now running at 12 per cent and may reach 14 per cent. That is intolerable. The report continues:
We do not know whether inflation can be kept this low. We rather doubt it and we do not know what kind of further social distortions will take place if inflation moves up to rates in excess of 10 per cent annually and middle income savings become subjected to confiscation by this rate of inflation.
The author of this report was a prophet. Today, mortgage funds are almost non-existent at rates which the average Canadian can afford. Now we have a bill before us which seeks to increase the borrowing level of trust and loan companies. That is how the government is trying to deal with the situation. We must go much further and consider the serious questions facing our entire banking structure. I am disturbed when I see advertisements dealing with guaranteed deposit certificates. What do they guarantee? They guarantee only the interest rate. Really, they guarantee the interest, and nothing else. I think that is intolerable.
Trust and loan companies are operating in the banking field. Legislation which controls banks guarantees the security of deposits. In this instance we are debating a bill which deals with guaranteed deposits, yet the guarantee really means nothing. Passage of this bill will increase the work load of the Department of Insurance because, obviously, more personnel will be needed in that department to supervise the operations of trust and loan companies.
It must be obvious, Madam Speaker, that we are fumbling around in speaking to this bill. The reason is simple. We have available absolutely nothing to help us debate this legislation. We are asked to rush this bill through without being able to make an effective contribution to

the debate. I hope that when the bill is discussed in committee the minister will make information available. In that way we could pass this bill rapidly, which I believe is what the minister wants. We can only discuss this bill intelligently if we have available adequate information.
This bill will increase the power of trust and loan companies which are not under the direct control of the Bank of Canada but which compete with banks in the field of banking. As I said earlier, the bill will apply to federally-incorporated institutions, and it is assumed that appropriate provincial legislation will follow. Let me ask this question: what steps has the government taken to make sure that legislation like this is applied uniformly across the country? How can we be assured of uniformity of legislation governing trust and loan companies? Certainly, the largest companies in the field are provincially-chartered. We should have before us information showing that the minister and his staff have discussed the matter with the provinces and that parallel legislation will be brought forward by the provinces, thereby bringing uniformity to the operations of trust and loan companies.
This bill will lower the safety margins of companies at a time when their assets are declining and their liabilities increasing directly because of inflation. Madam Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate. However, I have been inspired to do so by at least two factors. The first was well expressed by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling). Second-and I hope I do not have to apologize for being parochial-the matter of trust and loan companies is very personal to me and, I think, to many others from western Ontario. We-I include the parliamentary secretary-went through the traumatic experience of the failure some years ago of a very prominent trust company in our part of

Canada. It is easy for those of us who have practised law to regard a trust or loan company in a very narrow legal sense. Indeed, it is possible for those who have engaged in real estate, either as a member of the real estate profession or in conjunction with associates, to regard a trust company as merely a source of borrowing mortgage or shortterm funds. It is very easy for those of us who have the affluence with which to make substantial deposits to simply regard trust companies as a depository for those funds. However, I say to all hon. members that the ordinary Canadian, if indeed those whom I represent in Perth-Wilmot can be classified as such, regard a trust company as much more than that.
Those of us in western Ontario who invested funds in the company which failed some years ago regarded a trust company as almost akin to the Bank of Canada, not just for their deposit receipts, savings accounts or guaranteed investment certificates, but if one owned a share in a small rural trust company it was regarded as being almost fully guaranteed by the government. Shares in small trust companies, particularly those that were rurally-oriented, passed from generation to generation. I suspect this is true not only of western Ontario but of many parts of Canada.
The trauma and disturbance, not only to the economic community when one of these trust companies fails, is something you have to experience to appreciate. In the city of Stratford, people rushed to the trust company and literally took out suitcases full of money, for fear they would lose their entire savings. Loan share values went overnight to one-twentieth, and indeed one-fiftieth of their previous high values. When talking in terms of trust companies, I hope my colleagues will not regard them simply as financial institutions, because in many cases they are community institutions.
With regard to this legislation, I deplore the fact that it is prompted out of sheer necessity created by the cancer of inflation. No doubt we will have further legislation of a similar kind, because trust and loan companies find themselves in the horribly difficult position of having to pay tremendously high interest rates on even short-term money while at the same time trying to operate in a successful manner.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE HOUSEWIVES TO MAKE CONTRIBUTIONS AND TO COLLECT BENEFITS
speechtext:
that Bill C-202, to amend the Canada Pension Plan (housewives' contributions and benefits), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to enable housewives to make contributions to and collect benefits from the Canada Pension Plan. Since many housewives spend part of their careers working in industry as well as working at home, they should be permitted to continue their contributions to the Canada Pension Plan while at home to ensure them a full pension at retiring age. The bill
Canada Pension Plan
recognizes the equal importance of work performed at home with the work performed in industry and provides housewives with the same pension opportunities. The plan is voluntary and housewives are designated as selfemployed contributors paying the contribution of the employee as well as of the employer at the rate of their choice, up to the maximum.
Let us face it: in this country we can be very proud of the old age pension that has been a part of our life now for many years. We merely have to look back to the days when people reached old age and did not have security, to see how far we have come. Nevertheless, a great deal remains to be done. The old age pension is not high enough: it should be increased. The eligibility age should be lowered. People should be able to receive benefits at age 60.
A third point is that the Canada Pension Plan should be made applicable fairly to women and others outside the labour force. It is this third point which is the purpose of my bill. It could be argued that the Canada Pension Plan is not in the same package or is not in the same range as the old age pension; that the Canada Pension Plan is a work-related pension and that women who are not in the labour force, or others who are not in the labour force, should not have a claim on it.
When the plan was introduced, the argument was made that it was an actuarially sound plan. I do not think the Canada Pension Plan can be looked upon in that way. There is little relationship between the contributions and pensions. There is some relationship between the contribution the person makes and the pension he receives, but anyone can see there is a great benefit for people in a certain age group.
Anyone over 50, certainly, receives outstanding benefits from the Canada Pension Plan, when eligible, compared to a younger person. Our younger people are expected to contribute more to the plan than they could receive. They will have to nav a ereat deal more than they would have to pay for similar benefits in a private plan. There is a cross-subsidization in the Canada Pension Plan which in fact makes it a social plan rather than a straight plan or an actuarially-based plan.
The plan has been in operation since 1966. If a person were retired who had been paying in during these eight years, he would have paid in something under $800- actually, $779.40. He would begin to draw, in this year, $103 a month. This means that in less than eight months that person would have recovered all the contributions he had made to the plan. That is a pretty good deal for a person who retires at this particular time. It is pretty difficult to argue that this is an actuarially-based plan, because it was obvious from the day it was incorporated that people at certain age levels would receive considerable benefits.
Since it is an income support program in many ways, and since it involves a considerable subsidy from one element of society to another, why should housewives be excluded from the plan? What is the justification for saying it is strictly a work-related plan and, therefore, housewives who are supposed to be outside the regular work force have no claim upon it because they are not working in a factory, in the field, in construction or in

October 29, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
some other kind of industrial work? It is just not so. It is obviously a transfer payment.
The other argument is that it makes what I believe is a very serious distinction since it talks about work and refers to work related to industry. It would seem to be suggested that that type of work is fare more valuable in this country than work carried out at home. That is sheer nonsense. All of us recognize that that is not so, and that in fact the contribution of women in respect of raising children and maintaining a household may be far more valuable, in terms of the future of our country, than some obscure job or activity that men or women are now involved in.
There are many inconsistencies to be pointed out. I shall take just a few. Some men work very hard. I think most people in industry work pretty hard. But others have what are called very soft jobs, yet they can contribute and draw a pension because there is no way to evaluate such employment; there is no way of evaluating whether a person is working hard or has a very pleasant or unpleasant occupation. This bill does not, and should not, go into that because it is a very difficult judgment to make.
In some cases, however, we know that people are paid for doing work which is almost like leisure. Some people may put in only a couple of hours a week, yet they are in a position to draw full benefits. On the other hand, all of us are aware of women who on their own may raise a family of one, two or three children, which is a terribly difficult task. Why should such a woman not receive any benefit from the Canada Pension Plan? It seems to me that is a terribly unfair situation.
The Canada Pension Plan is a great improvement over what we had before it. I think most people feel it has worked out quite well. However, there are significant problems in respect of the plan. There are problems of equity and fairness about which I believe we should do something. The things I have said in respect of women apply to low earners and other people outside the labour force. Some men or women may not be in the work force because they are crippled, they may have disabilities which prevent their working, or they may have been ill during the latter part of their lives and therefore have not made contributions to the plan. These people are excluded from the plan. The same principle of unfairness applies in their case as in the case of housewives.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), on behalf of the government, has made a number of statements and has introduced legislation. He recognizes that this kind of anomaly exists. He has made a number of proposals to the House. It seems to me that none of those proposals is very satisfactory. They do not take into account some of the questions about fairness which arise in respect of the Canada Pension Plan. The chief proposal seems to be to take the amount of money that would normally go to the husband, and perhaps in some cases the wife, and split it so that each spouse receives an equal amount. That may satisfy a few technical draftsmen, but it will not change the picture very much, because all that will be done is to take from the husband in order to give to the wife; and that cannot be considered a very satisfactory arrangement.

The truth of the matter is that we really find it difficult to know how to correct these anomalies in the Canada Pension Plan. This leads me to the conclusion that either the government must find a way which will permit housewives and others to make contributions to and receive benefits from the plan on retirement on the same basis as those who are employed, or we may seriously have to consider-and I am certainly prepared to consider it-that the CPP and old age security program be combined into a universal pension at a much higher level. I mentioned that perhaps housewives and others should be subsidized by the government, but even if we have to subsidize some of the others-for instance, if there are poor people in our society who do not have the money to make their own contributions to the CPP-some method should be found to do it on their behalf.
I do not deplore the fact that we broadened the Canada Pension Plan; that may have been the only thing possible at that time. I know that my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), had a number of proposals which were better than the present CPP, but they were not acceptable at that time. There were problems with the provinces in trying to get their agreement on whether we would have a "pay as you go" plan or whether the plan should be funded.
A compromise was reached. Instead of a 20-year funding, we had a 10-year funding, but the "pay as you go" plan did not receive the support of the provincial governments. So it has come to the point where we have to review everything we are doing in the way of providing a pension for our senior citizens. Because if there is one thing that Canadians seem to agree upon, it is that we must look after the people who have spent so much of their lives in building up this country and providing the infrastructure and benefits which we have inherited. The Gallup polls which have been taken show that of all the programs, the one that is most universally admired and accepted, and the one that people are most willing to enlarge, is old age security.
I ask hon. members to consider this and, because of the importance of doing more for those who are retiring, to find a way of letting this private member's bill go to committee so that we can at least examine the serious questions that arise as a result of the present unfairness of the Canada Pension Plan.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, marriage is a partnership. When a couple enters into this holy state, they face a life ahead of them in which many decisions must be made. In some of these decisions they have a choice, but in other decisions they have no choice. To illustrate in which decisions they have no choice, let me refer to the decision of who will decide what the sex of the offspring will be. Another example is who will carry the offspring during the gestation period. At least medical science has not changed that yet.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE HOUSEWIVES TO MAKE CONTRIBUTIONS AND TO COLLECT BENEFITS
speechtext: You should bring in a bill to change that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE HOUSEWIVES TO MAKE CONTRIBUTIONS AND TO COLLECT BENEFITS
speechtext:
There are other decisions in which they do have a choice. To illustrate this, there is the decision as to

who will earn the income for the family unit. The husband may earn the income, the wife may earn the income, or they can both earn the family income. Another decision which they have the choice to make is who will do the housework. The husband can do it, the wife can do it, both can do it, or neither can do it but instead they can hire help to do it for them. In the latter case they have a real idea of the monetary value of the housework when they pay the wages of the help that does it.
So there is no question that housework has monetary value. The Canada Pension Plan is satisfactory unless that partnership breaks up; then the wife's contribution to the family unit to which her efforts have contributed are not recognized. I believe they should be recognized because there is a real value in these efforts that she has contributed to the family. This is why I support extension of Canada Pension Plan benefits to include housewives.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE HOUSEWIVES TO MAKE CONTRIBUTIONS AND TO COLLECT BENEFITS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE HOUSEWIVES TO MAKE CONTRIBUTIONS AND TO COLLECT BENEFITS
speechtext:
The question is, then: how can one achieve this? There are many options and many alternate ways of approaching this problem. One of the questions one has to consider is whether these contributions should be voluntary, or compulsory. Another question is whether one pension should be obtained, that is, split between husband and wife, or whether there should be two pensions, one for the husband and a separate one for the wife. There are several other questions but these are the two important ones that come to mind. So far as voluntary contributions to the CPP are concerned, the problem with this is that it tends to reward the rich, as they are the ones who can easily afford to make voluntary contributions, whereas the ones who will most likely need these benefits are the poor people who cannot afford extra premiums under the plan.
In actuarial terms, the Canada Pension Plan is not self-supporting, and this is a strong reason for there being just one pension spill Deiween husband and wife, uchuk two pensions would tend to double the amount of payments to be made and, therefore, worsen the financial imbalance and aggravate the problems we are facing in this inflationary period when we are trying to restrict government expenditures.
For this reason, it is important that we opt for the one pension plan split between two partners. It seems to me that when a family unit breaks up-which is a real tragedy-at that stage the court has to decide how the estate should be divided. Up to the present, it is my understanding that CPP benefits are not considered part of the estate, and therefore the wife cannot benefit and her efforts are not recognized. I think we should change this. It is my understanding that presently this matter is being considered by the government and that action will be forthcoming in the not too distant future. For this reason, I oppose Bill C-202 in its present form.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE HOUSEWIVES TO MAKE CONTRIBUTIONS AND TO COLLECT BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I say anything on the bill I should like to assure members of the House that the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine) is my seatmate, not my house spouse. I congratulate the hon. member for Waterloo-Cam-bridge (Mr. Saltsman) on his diligence in time and again
Canada Pension Plan
calling to the attention of the House, inequities which exist in the Canada Pension Plan. He is to be congratulated for bringing to the attention of the minister and the government the unfair situation which exists for the housewife. Also, I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) for the great concern he has shown in the ongoing development of the CPP. However, I am persuaded that both hon. members who have spoken in this debate are involved with the technical details of the implementation, and neither has come forward and recognized the ideological and philo-sosphical truths.
In the past, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge has said that if the housewife could make contributions to the plan or remain in the plan, the husband could pay for her if he were in a position to do so. Surely this is what a loving husband would do, without a plan. The hon. member is requesting that we seal forever in legislation the patronizing attitude which women have experienced through the years. He has also said, "If we cannot adapt the Canada Pension Plan to include housewives, then we must find a way of providing benefits and equity in the old age security benefit." Once again, is not each individual entitled to the old age security benefit? There should be no doubt that the house spouse, man or woman, should enjoy the equity of being entitled to Canada Pension Plan benefits. The minister has admitted that certain provisions within the plan accord different treatment to male and female contributors and beneficiaries. He has further recognized that views have been expressed that housewives who remain at home and do not draw salaries as members of the working force should be enabled to participate in the Canada Pension Plan.
The minister has suggested two approaches: first, crediting to the spouse remaining at home a portion of the
