tions made by the employer on the employed spouse's behalf; second, on an optional basis, permitting the spouse at home to contribute as a self-employed worker. Some hon. members who advocate the participation of housewives in the Canada Pension Plan appear to have two goals in mind: first, to give recognition to work in the home as regular employment; second, to guarantee some measure of independence to the housewife.
I must say I am convinced that hon. members then lose themselves in the technicalities of achieving these two goals. For my part, I would like to operate on the premise that all things are possible if we come to the proper conclusion concerning work and the independence of the housewife or housespouse. Let me address myself to these two matters and leave the legislation to far more competent individuals. Mr. Speaker, our recent rounds with inflation, unemployment, unemployment insurance and welfare, have brought much attention to the work ethic. Many statements have been made concerning the necessity for incentive programs and for the recognition of work, in itself, as a good thing. One such statement is as follows: To be idle is to become a stranger to the seasons.

October 29, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
To be idle is to step out of life's procession that marches in majesty and proud submission toward the infinite.
Life itself is pointless save when there is an urge.
The urge itself is blind save when there is knowledge.
Knowledge is vain save when there is work.
And all work is empty save when there is love.
And when you work with love you bind yourself to yourself and to one another and to God.
Mr. Speaker, you will notice that I have drawn freely on some of the great thoughts of Kahlil Gibran. It is most important to honour the work in the home, as all work in our day and age should truly draw honour. Work with love is to weave the cloth with threads drawn through the heart. It is building a house with affection. It is to sow seeds with tenderness and reap the harvest with joy. Surely hon. members will agree with me that housework is to charge all things you fashion with a breath of your own spirit. The work of the housewife is easily compared to the work of him who seizes the rainbow to lay it on a cloth in the likeness of man. Work is love made visible. This the housewife has done down through the centuries and we should be proud to recognize this along with the dignified work of the labourer, the executive, the soldier and the maestro.
Mr. Speaker, second I wish to address myself to the independence of the house spouse. I will, however, concentrate on the woman as the partner, because up to now she is the one who has been denied her independence. Marriage is that kind of experience which implies you were born together, and together you shall be forever more. But there should be spaces in togetherness. Again I quote:
And let the winds of the heavens dance between you.
Love one another, but make not a bond of love:
Let it rather be a moving sea between the shores of your souls.
Fill each other's cup but drink not from one cup.
Give one another of your bread but eat not from the same loaf.
Sing and dance together and be joyous, but let each one of you be alone.
Even as the strings of a lute are alone though they quiver with the same music.
Give your hearts, but not into each other's keeping.
For only the hand of life can contain your hearts.
And stand together yet not too near together:
For the pillars of the temple stand apart,
And the oak tree and the cypress grow not in each other's shadow.
I think back to the time when I was a young man and had the opportunity of observing a family which comprised 21 children and the father and mother. Certainly the father went to work, but I wonder what the mother with the 21 children did? Should her occupation not be classified as work? I think it is important to recognize that work in the house, that wealth for which mothers down through the ages have been responsible, is indeed dignified work, just as we have come to recognize that work with the shovel, with the pen, with equipment or even by automation is, indeed, an urge to move forward and to serve in life. So we must accept as a principle that work itself is dignified and that the housewife is, indeed, involved in work.
There is still some confusion, however. We are always unclear whether the woman is not still just part of the

family unit or whether she can have the option of going into a pension plan on her own without depending on the husband to pay her contributions. I believe that in most cases a loving husband takes care of his wife, so we are giving him the opportunity to do it in a legal fashion. It still leaves it up to the so-called senior partner, the head of the family, to decide if he will give the money.
Surely those persons who have some idea of technicalities can suggest a better settlement than this. Surely one of the main features of the Canada Pension Plan is its compulsory nature. Surely we should not settle in any way for the optional nature in respect of the woman. Surely we should not in any way try to secrete the money to her through the old age pension. Surely we should be proceeding with all haste to recognize the individual independence of woman, and that this woman is secure with this man and they are both entitled to the Canada Pension Plan, which may one day become a guaranteed income.
Mr. Speaker, let us not only in this House pass legislation concerning pensions. Let us make certain that we make an open statement concerning the dignified role of the housewife in our society. Let us make certain that, while recognizing the wonder and value of the family, we recognize the individual rights of its members, the participation and single desires of the husband, the individual rights of each child and the independence of woman to achieve her own destiny.
I am firmly convinced that in presenting legislation that touches on the status of women we must not continue to refer to women in a patronizing way, but as beings who deserve in every way equality with the breadwinner. To presume that men and women should always drink from the same cup, that they will always be united, is to presume that one or the other has lost his individuality. I believe in the perfect union where each should respect the other. Therefore we can refer to the term house-spouse. If, in future, the male decides to stay home and do housework, that term should apply to him. We must not lose sight of what we want to do.
In the past, the woman stayed home while the man went off and did what he had to do. The woman stayed home during wars; she stayed home and cared for 21 children while the man went to war, or the older brother went to war, or the older married son left his new wife and went off to fight. If we consider the task of woman to be work, let us dignify it. Let us pay her the respect we pay those who sent men to the moon; let us respect her in the way we respected those who, in generations of fear and oppression, defended nations. Let us respect her as we respect those who create paintings and music. Let us recognize that woman has prepared the supper with loving care, and performed with love those tasks which are necessary in the home, while others were away doing what they considered more important.
The minister, and the hon. member who presented this bill, have both shown great concern over improvements to be made to the Canada Pension Plan. I respectfully suggest that before we pass a measure of this kind, which is well deserved, we must respect work in the home as work
October 29, 1974

itself; we must respect the dignity and independence of woman.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE HOUSEWIVES TO MAKE CONTRIBUTIONS AND TO COLLECT BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments will deal with the comments of the two hon. members who have spoken, and with the voluntary aspect of the legislation in question. It has been suggested that for purposes of contributions the work of the housewife should not be considered as voluntary work but as regular employment.
For too long we have looked at the woman as the person who stays home and does housework and, at the end of the day, greets her husband and performs her wifely duties. It is time we considered providing some measure of financial security for the woman. I am thinking of women who may be deserted by their husbands, who may be separated from their husbands, or who may be divorced and are unable to obtain support from their ex-spouses.
The idea of bringing housewives under the umbrella of the pension plan was mentioned in Edmonton at the health ministers' conference last February. Since then this idea has become one of top priority. The matter is also under study by a subcommittee of the Canada Pension Plan Advisory Committee. Consultations between such bodies and those to do with the status of women have received a great deal of press coverage. We anticipate that reports will be forthcoming in the near future.
May I now talk about the hon. member's bill. As the hon. member knows, before a proposal like this can become law it must obtain the consent of two-thirds of the provinces containing two-thirds of the population. Therefore, the need for full consultation with the provinces before such a proposal can become law is clear. In addition, this subject is currently part of the total social security review being carried out by federal and provincial welfare ministers.
Another important consideration is die uou ability cf maintaining as much similarity as possible between the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan. For that reason I suggest that the implications of the present proposal should be discussed fully with representatives of Quebec who are also participating in the social review program.
Let me draw attention to another part of the hon. member's proposal. If a housewife's computed earnings are to be determined at her option, it surely follows that other contributors and non-contributors will demand the same right. Clearly, this implication of the hon. member's proposal would jeopardize the earnings related principle of the plan. For instance, if a housewife were allowed the right to determine earnings, there would be considerable pressure to allow the sole breadwinner the choice of increasing coverage from actual earnings to maximum earnings.
Another proposal concerns housewives being covered on a voluntary basis at the self-employed contribution rate. Presumably, coverage would be optional rather than compulsory, so as to avoid placing a burden on low income families. However, voluntary coverage, as proposed, would permit our more affluent families to contribute under the most advantageous circumstances. In other words, the
Canada Pension Plan
poor would not benefit and the rich, as they say, would get richer.
I think the bill defines to a certain extent the person who can be considered as a housewife, but does not say if coverage is to be extended to those involved in common law relationships, to house husbands, widows, and so on. Neither does it touch on the coverage of other deserving persons not attached to the labour force, such as students, non-working single women and the long-term unemployed.
The bill speaks of being occupied entirely as a housewife. Is it the intention to exclude any housewife who may earn a few dollars at some part-time activity? Some definition of parameters appears to be required in this bill. In other words you might have a housewife, who goes out and earns a nominal amount, being excluded from contributing as a housewife.
The whole bill seems to discriminate against an area of people who would like to be in the enviable position of being able to contribute to the maximum earnings without any set guidelines. The government, particularly the Department of National Health and Welfare, has been studying this whole area of trying to help the housewife.
The housewife has always been in a position in which she could not defend herself. She has not had access to legal facilities in the past. She has been doomed to the idea of going after welfare agencies for support, or of going after the stray husband. This has incurred an awful lot of difficulty, particularly where the woman could not receive any benefit until a certain period of time had elapsed.
The government has now come around in its thinking and some of the policies put forward in the working document which was presented by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to the standing committee on April 4, 1974, produced mandatory alternatives. These aUcinatives included the eor.+r^ntinn on earnings. This would allow a housewife to contribute in her own right and build up her own pension entitlement. However, it would be necessary to set a wage on what housewife duties are worth in terms of the family unit from which she comes. This approach would certainly give recognition to work in the home as regular employment. However, some standard would have to be obtained to make it non-voluntary in terms of any amount being contributed versus a set standard if this plan were to be used.
The other alternative is the splitting of pension credits, an approach set out by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. As the royal commission put it, this would involve crediting to the spouse remaining in the home a portion of the contributions of the employed spouse and of those contributions made by the employer on behalf of the employed spouse. This seems to be a fair way in terms of splitting the income of the earning spouse across the board in the event of a separation. In other words an agency could immediately go against the spouse and determine the amount the wife might have contributed at a designated point in time.
To explain it more clearly, the spouse would probably be entitled to a percentage of the earning spouses contribu-

Canada Pension Plan
tions at the time of the split. This means that if the husband decides to go, some agency will be able to go against his contributions and convert that to the benefit of the housewife.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Salts-man) is to be complimented on bringing forward this bill. However, the voluntary aspect is a handicap. It allows putting something into a pension plan on the part of a housewife that discriminates against her sex and others in the working world who would like to contribute on maximum earnings rather than the graded step.
To summarize, the government's position has already been stated. The government is studying the whole idea of pensions in relation to housewives. This became a priority at a meeting in Edmonton of the ministers of all provinces and the federal minister. It is being studied closely by the respective provinces as well as the federal government. Hopefully at some point in the future some type of legislation will be brought forward as a result of these studies.
As a result of that conference this whole issue was referred to the Status of Women Advisory Council as well as the Canada Pension Plan Advisory Council. They are studying the most advisable way of implementing a pension. Reports are anticipated, and implementation of the plan should be forthcoming.
I again thank the hon. member for his bill. However, I must oppose it on behalf of the government on the basis of the voluntariness of the plan. In one sense it is a very limited version of voluntariness. Also, the definition of housewife does not make it clear who would be included in this scheme. Someone could be excluded by working on a part-time basis. Even though she may not contribute to the Canada Pension Plan, she could be excluded under this bill. The voluntariness of the plan seems to discriminate against a lower income person whose husband cannot afford to give the benefit to the housewife to put into the plan. On the other side of the coin, there are those whose husbands earn sufficient to contribute to the maximum amount.
I am not trying to say that I am against the implementation of a pension for housewives. It is the position of the government that the work women do in the home will be recognized as regular employment and that they should be provided with protection against need. However, as I have said, the government is against this bill particularly on two points, the definition of "housewife" and of "volunteering" as put forward by the hon. member.

The fact that this debate is taking place today underlines how fast history moves. If any government were trying to bring in a bill today which left out of account, as the Canada Pension Plan does, the position of women in general, and particularly the position of housewives, it would have a rough ride. Yet only nine and one half years ago we debated and passed in this chamber the Canada Pension Plan with these deficiencies. A lot has changed in the last nine and a half years, and I pay tribute to those who have pressed the case of the rights of women to an equal place in our society.

I am glad this bill has been introduced. It is easy for the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Campbell) to call attention to the difficulties, but the issue will not go away and I do not think it would hurt the government to consent to the bill, or at least its subject matter, going to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs so that we could consider this whole question. It does seem to me that, in many respects, the position of women in relation to pensions has to be reviewed and updated.
As I say every time I get to my feet, I think it is for the birds that pension plans generally provide 100 per cent benefits to a man and provide for them to be continued at 100 per cent if he loses his wife and carries on, but provide only 50 per cent to the widow if the husband dies first. Likewise under the Canada Pension Plan there is a built in discrimination against the spouse, whether male or female. There is certainly a built in discrimination against housewives and I think this ought to be corrected.
This is private members' hour and one of the ten commandments for opposition members is never to be guilty of talking a bill out during private members' hour. So I will have to sit down soon. However, I do wish to express my congratulations to my hon. friend from Waterloo-Cambridge who has brought this issue forward today. I am not surprised that it is likely to be talked out, but I welcome the support from the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane), and from the parliamentary secretary for the idea that we should be coping with this problem. I just hope we cope with it soon.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure during the remaining few minutes of this debate to make a brief comment on the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman). I listened to his presentation and wish to be on record as being in agreement with most of what he had to say. It seemed to me, though, that the viewpoint he was putting forward was not broad enough-that amendments to the act should take into account other matters which are of equal importance.
I should like to express a special interest with regart to the position of women who are part of the management team on farms. These women have made a great contribution to the agriculture industry. For a while the trend in agriculture was toward large, integrated farms. Some may be surprised to learn that more of these farms went bankrupt on a percentage basis than any other type. It seems to be that the future of agriculture must be based on family management units, and when one thinks about family management units it is evident that a great deal of the input comes from farm wives.
I am talking now about viable farm units, units which are eminently successful, and to the operation of which the farm wife makes a major contribution as purchasing agent, registrar of pedigrees, and so on. If these groups are dissolved for any reason, the woman is at a great disadvantage; unless legal arrangements have been carefully made in advance she is likely to be left with little security and no recognition of the major contribution she has made. The same might be said of wives who help in the operation of small businesses.

We are not opposed to the position taken by the sponsor of this bill but, in our view, his proposals do not extend far enough, I should like to be recorded as saying that any person should have the right to contribute to a voluntary pension plan, whether a housewife, an injured workman, or a person who has had to withdraw from the work force for any reason. Finally, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for bringing his private member's bill before the House so that we might have an opportunity to discuss it.

Madam Speaker, there appears to be something odd and perhaps sinister about the manner and conduct of the debate on this bill. Quite frankly, it has been difficult for even the most astute technical financier to study and scrutinize any portion of the enormous verbosity and complexity of this bill. Its ramifications are tremendous and I sincerely fear that haste, in both perusal of the bill and a full and proper presentation of it, will sooner or later be regretted by those who have introduced it into this House.
There is a maxim in journalism and law which says: "When in doubt, leave it out". Possibly those who drafted this blooming legislation realized that it was not really blooming, and that they were following this maxim of when in doubt, leave it out. Perhaps we should do the same thing and throw the bill out this evening, because so much, Madam Speaker, is left hanging in mid-air. We are given no clues, and possibly those who drafted the bill had very few clues too.
So much of what should have been in the bill has been left out that the bill is made ineffective and meaningless. It is a terrible commentary on drafting. This legislation is a poor commentary on our parliamentary system. Those who presented Bill S-7, entitled "an act to authorize federal trust companies and loan companies to increase the monetary limit of their borrowing power and to issue subordinated notes," must have thought differently. They must have thought that the members of this House were very naive, to say the least.
First of all the title is misleading; it is deceiving; it is a misnomer. The explanatory notes and information given us by those presenting the bill are negligible. They are nil. It seems rather ridiculous for us to discuss any such legislation without having complete disclosure. In business circles one hears the expression "let us have disclosure". There is no disclosure in respect of this legislation.
The next item which concerns me, which must concern all other members, and which will disturb certainly decent thinking members of this House and the public when they hear of legislation of this kind, is the ministerial discretion that is given to some member of the cabinet. I thought that went out with Magna Carta when King John was taken to Runnymede. Certainly this bill will result in arbitrary, bureaucratic dictatorship for the minister, the trust companies and the loan companies.

This bill is a perfect example of the uselessness of the Senate and the duplication of cost to our country. It will lead to inflation. It is unreal. It will lead us into a worse economic situation than we have today. It is inflationary. Interest rates certainly are high enough, but if a bill of this kind should be enacted they will go even higher. I said earlier that the bill is a misnomer. Obviously this bill has been thrown together without any realization of its results and effects. My prediction is that it will create inflationary trends never seen before in Canada.
If this House should pass this bill, or even refer it to committee, that would be an absolute waste of time. There are other more important things which might be considered. There are many items in this bill that will lead citizens and shareholders alike to be misled in respect of subordinated notes. This is nothing more than a cheap way for loan and trust companies to obtain money from the citizens of this country without exercising a real responsibility toward them. There is no real protection provided for holders of these notes.
Again I urge that this bill not be sent to the committee but be voted out right now. It is a monstrosity.

Madam Speaker, as the hon. members for Nickel Belt and Moncton (Messrs. Rodriguez and Jones) have just explained, Bill S-7 is rather confusing. First of all, it was brought before this House after being passed by the Senate without our having had a chance to read it. We are being asked to pass a bill, and I quote:
-to authorize federal trust companies and loan companies to increase the monetary limit of their borrowing power-
-in order that they might loan and reloan at exorbitant interest rates, as we have quite often noticed in the field of finance.
To my mind, confusion reigns supreme in this country where financial and monetary matters are concerned: one day, plans are made to set up a federal development bank; the next, for another financial organization to confuse or annoy the people. Bill S-7 is yet another one, the purpose of which is to allow the trust and loan companies to borrow, and specially to increase their borrowing power.
To my mind, we are going around in circles; we are not improving the situation; on the contrary, there is more misunderstanding than ever about our present financial system.
Madam Speaker, we, of the Social Credit Party of Canada, have advocated for a long time a financial formula which some would call simplistic. I would rather have that than confusion such as is proposed by Bill S-7. I can understand that some hon. members oppose it, for instance, the hon. member for Moncton. He was not too clear about it when he said: We must oppose this bill. Why? No one knows. Still, the hon. members of the NDP applauded despite the fact that they did not know what it was all about.
However, the House studies the secondary aspects of the real problem, the secondary aspects of what must be changed in our economic system. And it is not by increasing the borrowing power of a loan company that we shall improve the situation. There are easier ways to do so.
October 29, 1974

As concerns Bill S-7, it is obvious that we oppose it and that we shall ask that it be put to a vote. The government has the majority, and this is the trouble with a majority government in Canada, Parliament is forced to accept its ideas while members of parliament should have all opportunities required to defeat the government on important matters, on monetary and economic matters, because all this is related to the Canadian economic system.
Madam Speaker, the Social Crediters have other solutions to suggest. Instead of increasing the borrowing power of federal trust and loan companies, we should use the services of the Bank of Canada, which belongs to Canada and to Canadian citizens, and harness the physical possibilities of our country. It is up to the government to pass regulations and to order the Bank of Canada to act in the interests of the Canadian people, and not in order to increase the borrowing power of federal trust companies or loan companies.
Instead of laughing at the duties and obligations of the Bank of Canada, all hon. members should force it to maintain an efficient instead of a restrictive economy, a logical instead of a shaky economy like the one we have presently. If we examined seriously the problem instead of creating new financial institutions and trust companies with increased powers, if we increased the powers of the Bank of Canada in order to serve the Canadian people, it seems to me it would be the end of the economic, political and social games we are witnessing at this time.
As everybody knows, there is a feeling of discomfort in all areas of economic activity. Let us correct the cause of this discomfort. I am sure it is possible to guarantee the Canadian people, without the help of any other country, economic security and personal freedom, and to ensure that Canadian production will first serve Canadians contributing to it.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this fairly straightforward bill is yet a somewhat significant one. I take pleasure in introducing it and recommending that it be sent to the Standing Committee on Agriculture where it can be examined further before proceeding into law.
Wheat Payments
This is a bill whose specific purpose is to enshrine for a period of years, in this case for seven years, a procedure whereby the treasury supplements payments made for wheat designed for human consumption in Canada. The government acted in order to place a portion of the cost of milling wheat essentially on the shoulders of the treasury, thereby minimizing the impact of increases in the price of wheat which were occurring, and ensuring that the price of bread, a product essential to the diets of families, particularly those with lower incomes, would be lower than would otherwise be the case.
The bill allows for the transfer from the treasury of up to $1.75 per bushel, with respect to wheat consumed in Canada, to the producers of the wheat-to the Wheat Board in the designated region, to boards designated in other regions to act on behalf of producers, or to producers themselves in other areas. The amount transferred is the amount they would otherwise normally have obtained from the millers.
Initially, the bill in the form in which it was introduced in the previous session would have performed this function for the full period of the arrangement which was entered into in September of 1973, in order to assure the transfer of the appropriate amount of money to the producers for the first part of the period. Before the passage of the bill an item in the estimates dealt with the first series of such payments, but the intention of the bill is to provide these payments for a long period of time.
I think it is significant that this payment in support of the price of bread is to be put into law for a prolonged period of time. It is in its present form without any doubt and, I should think without any argument, in the nature of a consumer subsidy, an amount paid by the treasury, on behalf of the people of Canada as taxpayers, to lighten the burden on the consumer of the cost of wheat products in Canada. It is in this way a significant milestone in tecn-nique, one which should be applauded by members on all sides of the House.
The bill also has a relationship to other factors in connection with wheat prices. The very title of the bill, two-price wheat, has had a fairly long history of debate in the producing areas of Canada, particularly in the prairie region where so much of our wheat is grown. There, when two-price wheat began to be talked about, it was in terms of the obligation and necessity of Canadian consumers paying a fair price for their wheat in Canada in order that producers receive a somewhat better return, even when the world price for wheat was lower than a figure that was reasonable in those days. The introduction of such a plan of higher prices for wheat was brought about in Canada initially, therefore, as a transfer from consumer to producers above that which the international market would bring them.
The first action in this regard was taken by this government in 1969, when the interruption in the arrangement made under the International Wheat Agreement meant that the world price began to fall below the floor that had been agreed upon. When that happened the government acted to hold the price in Canada at the figure of $1.9514, as it then was, which was the equivalent of the floor in the

international agreement. This price persisted, and was held throughout a period of very difficult years when the world price fluctuated but generally fell to levels in the order of $1.70 a bushel. Throughout that period two-price wheat was a benefit transferred from the consumer to the producer, but one which was fully legitimate, in my view and in the view of the government, due to the costs of production. Indeed, if it had been within our power we would have had such a price throughout the world market area rather than just in Canada alone.
Then in response to the suggestion that this was still inadequate, that further protection should be given the producer in connection with wheat consumed in Canada, and that further compensation could and should be given him, in 1972 we introduced a two-price wheat payment to farmers in addition to the $1.95'A that was being obtained by him from the market, a figure that was above the international price.
At that time, with the price still hovering in the area of $1.70 and with the price to millers at $1,951/2, we determined, in response to further requests from producer organizations, that a two-price wheat program should be brought in which, in effect, valued wheat consumed in Canada at $3 a bushel. Even at that time we showed our concern about the problem of imposing that additional cost on the actual consumers of bread, recognizing that so many of them were in the least suited position to pay, and that some of them would indeed require a helping hand rather than be given a further burden.
Accordingly in introducing the two-price wheat program we introduced it in the form of a payment from the treasury, rather than an increased charge from the millers. At that point we were in a situation where we effectively had a fixed price for wheat in Canada regardless of the world price. The $1.9514 would come from the millers and another $1.0414 would bring the amount up to $3; but we were effectively valuing wheat in Canada used for human consumption at a fixed price of $3 regardless of where the international price might be then.
With the changes in pricing patterns which occurred in 1973 and 1974, as international prices rose to the $3 level and then, indeed, passed that level, it became apparent that a review of the $3 price of wheat used for domestic consumption was appropriate. I suppose one could have taken the position that that having been the price which was set while the world price was as low as $1.70, it should have been maintained in a period after that while the world price rose above that price. However, we recognized that the producers had been in a difficult position, and that they were still in a difficult position in terms of their costs and their returns, and we accordingly felt that a different pricing structure was appropriate.
At that time, with prices approaching what were then record levels, levels which are still to this day pretty well close to a record, we decided that we should look at the proposition that as between the Canadian Wheat Board on the one hand, and other producers of wheat in Canada, and the consumers of Canada as represented by the buyers, millers and other users, we should enter into an arrangement whereby there would be a range of prices for grain, for wheat used for human consumption, a range

which reflected more adequately than anything before that the cost of production to producers.
Thus we decided that for seven years we would have a price of wheat in Canada for millers which would not be allowed to fall below $3.25, twenty-five cents higher than the previous fixed price, and correspondingly would not be permitted to rise above the level of $5. We recognized that with that arrangement there would possibly be transfers from producers to consumers compared with the world market when the price of wheat was above that $5 figure. On the other hand there would be potential transfers from the consumer to the producer in a period when the price of wheat was below $3.25.
It seemed to us that it was an appropriate time to enter into such an arrangement. From the producers' point of view it was a time when it was reasonable to look at long-term pricing in a way that would have been far less advantageous earlier. When prices are low it is very hard to persuade buyers to enter into agreements which include price ranges that are very high. At the time we entered into this arrangement we had prices that had just hit a record level, a level which, as I have pointed out, is today still a record. For only very brief periods has the price of wheat crossed the level which we had at the time this arrangement was entered into, Mr. Speaker.
What we were doing was saying that this kind of arrangement is one that we would like to enter into with some of our regular customers, a long-term arrangement whereby a reasonable range of prices for grain was fixed, a range that recognized cost of production of this grain on the part of the producer. Having set the range at $3.25 to $5 for a seven year period, we continued the philosophy that had gone into the original payment from the treasury for two-price wheat, namely, that the portion above $3.25 should be borne by the treasury rather than be reflected in an increase in the price of bread.
At that time as we made our move we were able, in effect, to stop the price of bread moving on the basis of increases in the price of wheat. The price of wheat was just moving through the floor level in terms of the millers' business when we entered into this arrangement. We therefore decided to put forward the proposition that while wheat, in terms of bread wheat other than Durum, was above $3.25, the portion higher than that 'up to $5 should be paid for from the treasury.
In the case of Durum, while the arrangement was just a little different, the basic principle was the same with a payment up to $1.75 from the treasury, although there the actual price in play went higher and this was also reflected in the amount allowed to be obtained from the millers. In our view the price for Durum was unnaturally separated from the price for other wheats, and there is a common long-term floor of $3.25 which was adopted for both.
This then is a measure which will see the transfer to producers from the treasury, for the period of the full seven years originally intended of amounts of money which will save the consumer significant amounts in the cost of his bread.
Figures can perhaps be a little misleading in talking about the price of bread because this depends upon mark-
October 29, 1974

ups and the arrangements that different people in the producing and marketing chain have, but I think one can safely say that this particular measure, with world prices at or above the $5 level, is saving in the cost of flour for bread in the order of five cents or six cents a standard loaf. To that extent it continues to be perhaps a small but significant element in our effort to cushion the problem of the cost rise for those who have to bear the load.
I, therefore, commend this measure to hon. members and invite them to pass it to the committee where we can look at it more specifically. Then we can see the bill become a part of the law of the land. As I said at the beginning, I believe it is a simple and straightforward measure.
I think this is a significant measure in the way of enshrining into our law a consumer subsidy for a significant period of time. I commend the measure to all hon. members and urge its passage on second reading for later study in the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset may I say that we on this side of the House agree with the principle of a two-price system. We regret, however, the fact that this bill lacks an effective measure to take into consideration the increased costs of production. Therefore we would recommend to the minister the implementation of such a provision to reflect the rising costs of production over the seven-year period.
The absence of such a mechanism is tantamount to a seven-year freeze for the Canadian wheat farmer in the range between $3.25 and $5 a bushel, depending upon world markets, in the case of wheat, and $5.75 to $7.50 in the case of Durum. So, it seems to me that at this point in time, during this period of very rampant increases in the costs of production, and during a period of very rampant inflation, more effective measures should be instituted in the pricing structure to take into consideration the increases in Droduction costs. I do not believe that the range referred to by the minister truly reflects or takes into consideration such increases in the costs of production because that range would be utilized depending only upon the price in world markets.
The minister has suggested that this measure constitutes a subsidy to the consumer at the expense of the public treasury. The minister may have referred to this and I may have missed it, but I would suggest that it also constitutes a subsidy at the expense of the producer, because we know that at this time the export price for milling wheat hovers in the $6 range while producers are receiving $5 per bushel for wheat earmarked for domestic human consumption.
It seems to me we really are asking too much of the wheat producer in respect of this bill. We are asking him to accept the vagaries of the international market place. This is something which, in the absence of any long-term international wheat agreement, the producers must bear the brunt of Mr. Speaker. Now we are asking the wheat producers to absorb the inflationary effects of a government which has no anti-inflation policy to speak of and I do not believe it is right to ask producers to accept the increase in farm input costs over which this government has exercised absolutely no control, and in respect of which it has shown no leadership.
Wheat Payments
The increase in input costs, has been averaging about 20 per cent on an annual basis. The producers have had to bear the brunt of this while the government played the role of Santa Claus with the unions. It is certainly a lot to expect the wheat producers to accept this as well as the uncertainty which surrounds the transportation system and the threat of the loss of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. They are also being asked to absorb the huge demurrage costs which have accumulated. It seems to me that to ask them to do all these things is really asking too much from the wheat producers of Canada.
If we are dealing with a legislative measure which is supposed to give some protection and some stability to the wheat producers of the country, certainly now is the opportune time to build into the legislative mechanism some protective features which would offset the spiralling costs which face the western wheat producers.
We know, for example, that the two-price system which has been in effect for some time now has already cost the producers something in the order of $15 million. That represents the difference in the amount the producers could have received had the wheat been sold on the export market rather than being used for domestic consumption. As I said before, in the international market the export price for milling wheat is in the $6 per bushel range, while wheat which will be earmarked for domestic human consumption will be frozen at a maximum of $5 a bushel.
Canadians consume for human consumption something in the order of 60 million bushels of wheat per year. The difference of $1 per bushel between the export price and the domestic human consumption price will mean that, over the period of the next 12 months, the producers in western Canada in effect will be losing something in the order of $60 million. So, having regard to the fact that wheat producers are indeed giving up very much under this bill, it seems to me it would not be asking too much that the minister and the government build in an effective indexing system which would retlect the increases in ihe costs of production on a year basis.
I am not sure whether the minister feels that prices on the international market will maintain their high level or will go down. Nevertheless, it seems to me that if we do not bring forward some measure in this area, the producers in this country, having regard to the fact that prices on the international market may go down, could find that a bushel of wheat will be back to $3.25. It seems to me also-and I want to remind the minister again-that it is because of the absence of an effective cost of production control that we opposed quite vigorously the stabilization bill. I am sure that if the minister again introduces a grain stabilization bill in the House it would be in his best interest to propose some sort of mechanism to deal with the increases in the costs of production.
The United States, in its stabilization agricultural programs, has incorporated an indexing provision related to the costs of production, to ensure the wellbeing of farmers. This is also another reason why we should be going in that direction. Indexing has become a fact of life in Canada with this government, just as inflation is a fact of life. However, the government continues to say that it cannot

October 29, 1974
Wheat Payments
do much about inflation because it is an international phenomenon. But really what we are doing here is, in effect, fighting inflation on the backs of the farmers by not providing an effective mechanism which would cushion the effects of inflation upon them.
I must say again, as I said at the outset of my remarks, that the price of wheat for domestic human consumption is in effect being frozen. It is rather interesting that we have two vital commodities in western Canada being frozen, namely, wheat and oil-both products of the west-and yet the minister, whose interest in western Canada is known, and in spite of the fact that the government is not prone to accept the concept of price freezes, allows the price of both these important commodities produced by western Canada to be frozen for the benefit of the consumers in the whole of Canada.
It is also very disturbing to me to note that the minister suggests that he will examine the Crowsnest freight rates which for years have been the Magna Carta to western grain producers. In this respect we get conflicting comments from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and the minister responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang). I hope that the minister will outline the form that the review of these rates will take, and that he will outline the policy upon which the government has embarked with regard to grain handling and transportation.
I also hope that very soon the promise of an equalized freight rate structure-a promise which was made to western agricultural ministers a year or so ago-according to which we would get better freight rates on the movement of beef from western to central Canada, will be kept. We certainly hope that the government will act more quickly than it has in the last twelve months with regard to the removal of the various freight rate anomalies and inequities which have existed in the country for the last 18 months, and which have been the subject of debate in the House.
I think that this bill could be improved if the minister would accept the amendments which I have outlined. If that were done, I think the bill would be a very good bill for western Canadian wheat producers as it would give some stability to the domestic grain trade. As it stands in its present form I do not believe this legislation gives the western wheat producer a fair deal.
There is something else that I would like to say in connection with wheat. It seems to me that the initial price is far too low in terms of current prices on the international market, as well as in terms of the domestic market. I urge the minister to undertake an adjustment immediately.
I just had a call from a producer in Vermilion who told me that he was getting $1.80 per bushel for wheat which he was selling to an elevator through the Canadian Wheat Board. He could sell the wheat as feed for $2.80, although it is not feed wheat. Many producers are uncertain as to what route they should take, and they are looking for guidance.
Surely, with the prices in the $5 to $6 range, it seems to me only reasonable to request that an upward adjustment be made quickly because now is the time when producers need money to pay their farm expenses, to settle their

debts, and to prepare for a long, but I hope, not cold winter.
I should like to conclude by saying that I hope the minister will seriously consider the comments that I have made, and will decide to help the western wheat producers at a time when it is urgent to do so, because I fear that the wheat that has been harvested this year is of a much lower grade than usual and, as a result, will bring in lower prices which will have a detrimental effect on the gross and net incomes of the producers.
Many grain producers and small livestock producers find themselves in a difficult situation. An adjustment of the initial price, as well as some assurance of a stable wheat market, at least on the domestic scene, would certainly provide the kind of climate that is conducive to a strong and healthy agriculture.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-19 before us this evening is almost identical to Bill C-33 which died in the last parliament. The only difference between them is the date at which they come into force. Bill C-33, with which we would have dealt in the last parliament, would have come into force several months earlier, but last Friday parliament voted, in supplementary estimates, the money for the previous several months, with which we will not deal so far as this bill is concerned.
The bill before us today basically does two or three things. It establishes the floor price for the next seven years for wheat and Durum. The floor price is a guarantee of what the farmers, no matter what happens to the international price of wheat, will receive for wheat that is sold domestically. I think it is a step that all members of the House support in principle, and it is one that our party has advocated for many years. Before I entered politics I remember hearing a spokesman for our party call for a two-price system and price guarantees. Members of the cabinet at that time dismissed it as socialistic nonsense, something that was completely impractical. One of the chief detractors was, as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) says, a Saskatchewan Senator. Now this Utopian nonsense is becoming law. Perhaps the pressures of the last parliament forced the government to wake up to the needs of the western farmer.
The subsidy provided in the bill is $1.75. That means that if the price for international grain is $3.25, with the subsidy the farmer will receive $5 a bushel. If the guaranteed price for Durum wheat is $5.75, with the subsidy of $1.75 he will receive $7.50 a bushel.
It should be stressed that it is not only the consumer who is paying for this type of legislation. As has already been made clear by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), the farmer is taking a loss because of the present two-price system. From some figures I saw last Saturday I noticed that wheat is selling for $6.04 on the international market. That is about a dollar above the price the farmer is getting for domestic grain sold for human consumption. It means that the government is making a sacrifice in order to keep the price of bread
October 29, 1974

down. This is basically a good step, but it should be made permanent.
The whole philosophy of price guarantees and price supports should be applied to all farm products. The principle is sound. If there were price guarantees farmers would be able to plan in the spring-f.or what they would receive in the fall. The farmer gambles on the weather, on world conditions, on the international market; why he should have to gamble with government programs is beyond me.
I should like to see an amendment moved in committee to provide for the indexing of the price to the farmer for wheat consumed domestically. Maybe we should index the floor price, or the government subsidy, or the ceiling price. If not, the farmer could find the price of grain frozen for seven years while his costs of production skyrocket. Perhaps there could be indexing in the manner that has been developed for taxation, old age pensions, family allowances and such things. The basis of the index could be the increase in the costs of production. The alternative would be a clause in the bill to provide for review by the House of Commons each year. If an upward adjustment were necessary, then this House would make it.
Another point is that we should provide for policing of the bill. One of its purposes is to provide a consumer subsidy so that an increase in the price of wheat will not necessarily mean an increase in the price of bread. When there are subsidies or taxcuts on items like clothing or children's footwear the saving is not always passed on by the wholesalers or retailers, but is sometimes regarded by them as extra profits or dividends for their shareholders. This legislation should be policed to make sure that that does not happen with this subsidy. It is not intended for the companies, for Weston's or any other miller.
This legislation was first announced in September, 1973, Womhor tVwa millers annntinrpd that the Drice of a loaf would be increased by four cents. After pressure from this House and the Food Prices Review Board, the increase was rolled back to two cents. Despite the fact that the price of wheat had not gone up, in August, 1974, the millers announced that the price of a loaf would go up by three cents in the middle of September. So, since this legislation was introduced the price of bread has gone up by five cents a loaf despite the fact that the price of wheat has not increased. We are aware that there are many other inputs in the price of a loaf, but I wonder whether the five-cent increase reflects the legitimate costs to the bakers.
If we pass this legislation it seems to me that the Food Prices Review Board or some such body should police it to make sure that someone is not pocketing the subsidy at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer.
Those are some of the concerns I have about the bill, Madam Speaker. We support it in principle, but we should keep in mind that it is only a small step, toward providing the farmers of western Canada and the other wheat producers with income security. We must have a stabilization plan to cover all products and to take into account the increased costs of production. Unless we have that, farmers will not be able to continue in business.
Wheat Payments
We just have to look around the world to see how people are starving. This should be one of the first considerations of the food conference in Rome in November.
There should be price guarantees, floor prices, price supports on all farm products whether consumed domestically by human beings, or exported. If we do this we will not only help the Canadian farmer but will be playing our part in the world as a great food producing nation.
We must also consider the very low initial payment when we talk about wheat. Wheat is now selling in the world market for about $6 a bushel, yet farmers in my area are getting only $2 per bushel initial payment because the Wheat Board is holding back $4. That is like saying to any worker that a half or two thirds of his income will be held until the end of the year, and then paid to him without interest. How would members of parliament react if 50 per cent of their salary were held back for nine or ten months and then paid without interest? Yet that is the way we are treating our farmers, and it must be changed. I hope the minister will have an announcement on it shortly.
Another thing that concerns me is that the initial price of feed grains is being held down and, as a result, many farmers are going to the open market where they get a higher price for grain delivered on the spot. It seems to me that there is a sly hand in this. I am suspicious of why the minister is not raising the initial price of feed grains, and wonder if he is trying to drive farmers to the open market so that he can then say that they do not use the Wheat Board. The government wants to sell feed grain on the open market. Obviously it does not want the Wheat Board, and thinks that perhaps we should get rid of it. Mr. Speaker, my question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) of October 3 was prompted by statements that were made by two ministers, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) and the then minister of fisheries, Hon. Jack Davis, during the July 8 election campaign. The statements in question concerned the Law of the Sea Conference and the action allegedly proposed by the government if our country's position with respect to jurisdiction over our off-shore resources was not accepted by the member nations represented at the conference.
Both ministers are reported to have said categorically that the government was prepared to act on its own and declare unilaterally its jurisdiction over the continental shelves off our coasts. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion made the statement in Corner Brook, Newfoundland, on June 24, at a political rally at which the Prime Minister was present. The former minister of fisheries, Mr. Davis, made a similar comment in a statement which was prepared by him in Vancouver and released in Halifax on June 15, to coincide with the closing meeting being held there of the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries, ICNAF.
In reply to my question of October 3 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) questioned the accuracy of the press reports to which I referred. At the same time he stated

speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION OVER COASTAL WATERS-POSSIBILITY OF UNILATERAL ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that what he said in closing is not correct. We will not let the fishing industry down.
The question has been raised whether Canada should now proceed unilaterally and extend its fishing jurisdiction to the edge of the continental shelf. As the House is aware, Mr. Speaker, the world community is presently engaged in bringing the Law of the Sea in line with the political and economic realities of our times.
A first session of the Law of the Sea Conference was held last summer in Caracas. Given the large number of participating countries, over 135, and the many complex issues to be resolved, it was not possible to elaborate, in all its details, a treaty dealing with all the aspects of the subject.
However, during the Caracas session real progress was achieved. It became apparent that a future Law of the Sea Treaty could only be agreed upon if coastal states were recognized as having effective rights with respect to both
Adjournment Debate
living and mineral resources, as well as for the protection of the marine environment. These rights will be exercised by the individual coastal state in an "economic zone", which is generally conceived as extending to 200 miles from the coast. However, the question of whether such rights would go beyond the 200-mile limit and reach the edge of the shelf did not receive the same degree of support as was given the economic zone concept. Canada is, however, hopeful that some arrangement can be worked out in this sense.
In these circumstances would it be timely for Canada to extend its fishing jurisdiction unilaterally? I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that, as a responsible member of the international community, Canada should aim at a widely accepted Law of the Sea and, as a consequence, should give the United Nations Law of the Sea Conference a chance to succeed. We are confident that it will. This does not mean that the government is not conscious of the need to prevent over-exploitation of the living resources off our coasts, even before the conference ends. Indeed, through action as a member of international bodies such as ICNAF, as well as through bilateral consultations, the government is constantly trying to control this situation.
The best way for Canada to acquire sufficient powers to remedy this problem is through international agreement. In present circumstances unilateral action would only create confusion and controversy. I would also add that control of the living resources over the continental margin would fall short of providing adequate protection for salmon. That particular issue also calls for international acquiescence in the rights of the state of origin.
In brief, Mr. Speaker, unilateral action, though not called for at the moment, could very well be considered as a matter of policy if the Law of the Sea Conference fails, within a reasonable period of time, to reach a satisfactory solution as regards the interests of coastal states in their offshore living resources. subtopic: STORMS-ATLANTIC PROVINCES-REQUEST FOR AID FROM PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
STORMS-ATLANTIC PROVINCES-REQUEST FOR AID FROM PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is well known that I participate frequently in what is called the "Late Night Show". Some people ask why, and the answer is that I am a great lover of crowds and there is nothing like a large and enthusiastic audience to turn me on.
A few days ago I asked a question about the measures being taken to assist the people of Prince Edward Island who suffered severe crop damage, besides loss of electricity and telephone services, as a result of a severe storm in what is well know as the garden province. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Cullen) seemed to be well briefed on the issues and I congratulate him on the lucidity, fulsomeness and directness of his reply. He might well serve as a model to other parliamentary secretaries, and indeed to those lofty incumbents of the treasury benches.
870

October 29, 1974
Adjournment Debate
A great many islanders were seriously inconvenienced for a period of a week and, in some cases, for a little longer. Shortages of utilities, water, light and fuel made life difficult for the people and for their farm animals. There was a threat to our valuable potato crop and to such grain as was not harvested. I now hear less disturbing reports than were coming my way when I first asked the question. Yet to many people this was not an inconvenience of a minor nature. For a week it was impossible to telephone to my residence in Prince Edward Island, as I discovered daily. Many homes were unheated for days. The utility companies moved as best they could to get things back to normal.
My main concern has to do with the alacrity of the movement of aid toward provinces and regions affected by seriously adverse weather conditions. From time to time in this House I have heard members bring forward appeals arising from emergency situations in their home areas, inquiring about federal aid and being advised that no official request had yet come from the province concerned. In many cases speed is of the essence, and I would urge greater co-ordination so that there might be a diminution of the waiting period.
In July of this year a freak storm damaged crops in my constituency. Appeals for compensation were made, discussed and processed, but it was a long time before the victims of the storm were able to receive funds, or even to receive assurances as to the measure of aid which would come to them. In these days it is not easy to wait. Time is money, and during a period of inflation money is shrinking.
It is ironic I should be talking about two grim assaults from nature on Prince Edward Island-strange, because this summer was one of the most beautiful and balmy in the island's history, as many thousands of tourists can testify. I appeal for a method whereby the whole procedure for making aid available in such cases can be improved and expedited.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: STORMS-ATLANTIC PROVINCES-REQUEST FOR AID FROM PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his kind comments. One of the things which make this country great is the fact that although there is a problem in Prince Edward Island the heart of the rest of the country goes out to the people there in the disaster they face.
Federal policy on disaster assistance has, since 1970, taken the form of reimbursing provincial governments on the basis of a per capita formula for the expenditures made by the provinces in dealing with a disaster. It seems to indicate that kind of thrust the hon. member seeks, and I am sure all hon. members seek, in dealing with disasters or problems in their immediate areas. But the initiative must be taken by the province to determine the size of the disaster and the kind of assistance that is required, and then it must make an application to the federal government.
There is, however, as the hon. member knows, a formula set up for the sharing of the cost, and the formula is equal to the amount of $1 multiplied by the population of the province. When the sum exceeds that amount there is an ever increasing formula of contribution at the federal level.
Generally speaking, eligible expenditures are those made by a province for the restoration of essential property of private individuals, small businesses and farmsteads, and public works, to their pre-disaster condition. These guidelines limit cost sharing for agricultural losses to payments made to restore farmlands to workable condition where a farm operation has been seriously affected by flood erosion or land gouging.
Payments made for the restoration of farm buildings and equipment would also be eligible, since they would represent payments made for restoring the essential private property of the farmers concerned. The basic federal measure for assisting farmers who suffer losses on account of damage to farm products is the Crop Insurance Act. This act is given effect by means of the federal-provincial crop insurance agreements which have been contracted between the federal government and the various provinces.
I think it is fair to say that Prince Edward Island has sought advice on what provincial expenditures, related to the earlier storm of July 3, would be eligible for cost sharing. If a similar request is received from Prince Edward Island regarding expenditures related to the recent storm, it will receive prompt and sympathetic consideration. But the initial thrust, as the means of expediting assistance, has to come from the province, which has to determine the size of the disaster and the amount of funds it is seeking.
